curations.original_notes: later readings connect promise and blessing to Christ
curations.textual_observation: Galatians 3:6–29 connects Abraham’s blessing with the nations and identifies Christ as the promised “seed” in Paul’s argument.
curations.uncertainty: Galatians 3 is Paul's later reception of the Abraham traditions; it should be distinguished from the original literary setting of Genesis.
curations.why: This is Paul’s later scriptural interpretation of the Abraham promise; distinguish it from Genesis’s own wording.

curations.textual_observation: The Black Obelisk depicts a tribute bearer identified in its inscription as Jehu of the House of Omri; 2 Kings 10 narrates Jehu’s reign but not this tribute.
curations.uncertainty: The Black Obelisk's tribute image is Assyrian royal representation and does not supply a complete account of Jehu's reign or Israelite policy.
curations.why: The monument supplies external evidence about Assyrian royal representation, not a detail reported by 2 Kings.

curations.textual_observation: Sennacherib’s prism records his campaign against Judah; 2 Kings 18:13–17 likewise introduces his invasion and the siege of fortified cities.
curations.uncertainty: The background cluster compares Assyrian annals with Kings and Isaiah; their accounts are distinct royal and Israelite/Judean textual witnesses.
curations.why: The prism is an Assyrian royal account and the Kings passage a biblical narrative; their claims and rhetoric differ.

curations.uncertainty: The Black Obelisk records Jehu's tribute in Assyrian royal language; its absence from the brief Kings account is not evidence that tribute did not occur.

curations.original_notes: Assyrian terminology links Jehu with the land or house named for Omri.

supporting_ckl_sources.author: Nimrud: Materialities of Assyrian Knowledge Production project
supporting_ckl_sources.title: The Black Obelisk of Shalmaneser III

curations.textual_observation: The Black Obelisk calls Jehu “son/house of Omri”; 2 Kings 10 identifies Jehu as Israel’s king but does not use that Assyrian designation.
curations.uncertainty: The phrase 'house of Omri' is Assyrian political terminology associated with Israel and Jehu; it should not be treated as a precise synonym for the city of Samaria.
curations.why: The inscription reflects Assyrian naming practice; it should not be treated as a precise biblical or modern geographic label.

curations.original_notes: prophets anticipate the Messiah
curations.textual_observation: Deuteronomy 18:15–22 promises a prophet like Moses and gives criteria for distinguishing true from false prophetic speech.
curations.uncertainty: Prophetic texts have varied historical settings and later Jewish and Christian readings; the curation does not claim every prophet predicts one figure in the same way.
curations.why: The passage grounds prophetic expectation; its identification with the Messiah is a later interpretation, not explicit here.

curations.original_notes: resurrection inaugurates the kingdom’s future
curations.textual_observation: In 1 Corinthians 15:24–28 Paul describes Christ handing the kingdom to God after the defeat of hostile powers, with resurrection as the preceding argument.
curations.uncertainty: This is a thematic connection in Paul's account of resurrection and the handing over of the kingdom, not a claim that the two themes are identical.
curations.why: The passage directly joins resurrection hope and the kingdom’s consummation.

curations.original_notes: God’s reign fully revealed
curations.textual_observation: Revelation 21:1–5 depicts a new heaven and earth, with God dwelling among people and death no more.
curations.uncertainty: Revelation 21 depicts the renewed city and God's presence; the authored kingdom connection is thematic, since the passage does not call the city itself 'the kingdom.'
curations.why: The vision connects the New Jerusalem with the kingdom theme through divine presence and the end of death.

curations.original_notes: The cultural-background cluster compares the annals with biblical tribute notices and Assyrian royal media.

supporting_ckl_sources.author: A. Kirk Grayson and Jamie Novotny
supporting_ckl_sources.title: The Royal Inscriptions of Sennacherib, King of Assyria (704-681 BC), Part 1

curations.textual_observation: Sennacherib’s prism records the king’s campaign in Judah; the cluster places this annal beside biblical siege accounts and Assyrian royal media.
curations.uncertainty: The prism preserves Assyrian royal annals, whose campaign account emphasizes tribute and does not claim Jerusalem was captured.
curations.why: This is contextual comparison, not an assertion that the annal confirms the biblical account.

curations.original_notes: prophetic messianic expectation
curations.textual_observation: Deuteronomy 18:15–22 speaks of a prophet like Moses and tests prophetic claims.
curations.uncertainty: Deuteronomy 18 concerns a prophet like Moses in its own setting; identifying later messianic expectation is a reception and interpretation, not an uncontested original reference.
curations.why: This supports a thematic link between prophecy and messianic expectation only at the level of later interpretation.

curations.original_notes: resurrection and reign
curations.textual_observation: 1 Corinthians 15:24–28 describes Christ’s reign and the handing over of the kingdom to God.
curations.uncertainty: 1 Corinthians 15:24-28 connects resurrection hope with the Messiah's reign; it does not by itself define the complete scope or timing of the kingdom.
curations.why: It links kingdom and resurrection within Paul’s argument; resurrection is developed in the surrounding chapter.

curations.original_notes: Jesus' death is read through Passover
curations.textual_observation: In 1 Corinthians 5:7–8 Paul calls Christ “our Passover” and urges the community to keep the feast with sincerity and truth.
curations.uncertainty: Paul's Passover language is a later Christian interpretation of Jesus' death. It does not make the Exodus setting and crucifixion event identical or settle every aspect of the metaphor.
curations.why: Paul explicitly interprets Christ’s death through Passover imagery in this passage.

curations.original_notes: adoption is central to identity in Christ
curations.textual_observation: Romans 8:14–17 describes those led by the Spirit as God’s children and heirs with Christ.
curations.uncertainty: Romans 8 describes adoption and the Spirit's witness; later theological formulations should not be read back as the only meaning of Paul's language.
curations.why: This links identity in Christ with adoption language in Paul’s argument.

curations.original_notes: holy identity leads to holy conduct
curations.textual_observation: 1 Peter 2:9–12 calls its addressees a holy people and urges conduct that can be observed by outsiders.
curations.uncertainty: The passage links communal identity with conduct. The curation does not treat holiness as a status earned by behavior.
curations.why: The passage joins communal identity to holy conduct.

curations.original_notes: identity in Christ is personal and corporate
curations.textual_observation: 1 Peter 2:9–10 applies Israel’s people-language to its addressees, calling them a chosen race and people who received mercy.
curations.uncertainty: The cited text combines personal allegiance with corporate identity; it does not reduce identity in Christ to either individual or group identity alone.
curations.why: The text supports the corporate dimension of identity; it does not reduce identity to an individual status.

curations.original_notes: David and the Psalter
curations.textual_observation: Psalm 110 bears a Davidic superscription and depicts the addressed lord’s enthronement and priestly status.
curations.uncertainty: Psalm 110 bears a Davidic superscription in the received text; the superscription does not prove modern claims about the psalm's date or authorship.
curations.why: The superscription is the Psalter’s attribution; it is not independent evidence about David’s authorship or biography.
